title: 📘 UNIT 8: POLITICAL, SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC PROCESSES IN ETHIOPIA, MID-16th TO MID-19th C.
notes:
📅 Period: Mid-16th to mid-19th century

After the decline of the Christian Kingdom, many peoples in southern, western, eastern and central Ethiopia developed independent local states and political systems.

title: 📌 8.1 PEOPLES AND STATES OF THE EASTERN, CENTRAL, SOUTHERN AND WESTERN REGIONS
notes:
From the mid-16th to mid-19th centuries, many Ethiopian peoples were politically autonomous and independent polities flourished.

🏛️ Political organization varied from centralized monarchies to traditional systems of governance.

🤝 Relationships among peoples and states included:
• Trade
• Marriage
• Competition over resources
• Warfare
• Cultural interaction

These interactions could lead states to expand their territories or lose them.

title: 📌 8.1.1 SOUTHERN STATES
notes:
The southern region contained several Omotic and Cushitic peoples and states with different political, social and economic systems.

📌 Major groups and systems discussed:
• Omotic states under Tato system
• Omotic states under Kawo/Kati system
• Cushitic states under Sera-Woma system
• Gurage chiefdoms
• Siltie Sera

title: 👑 Omotic States & Peoples Under the Tato System
notes:
The Tato system characterized states such as Kafa and Yem.

👑 Tato → title used for the king.

📌 Main characteristics:
• Hierarchical political organization
• Kingship
• Councils of advisers
• District chiefs
• Agriculture and trade
• Strong territorial organization

title: 🌿 Kafa Kingdom
notes:
📍 Located south of the Gojeb River and north of the Omo River.

👑 King → Tato
🏛️ Capital → Bonga
🏙️ Second centre → Anderecha

The kingship was hereditary, but the Mikkerecho council selected the successor from the king's sons.

🏛️ Mikkerecho:
• Council of nobles
• Assisted the king
• Helped select successors
• Administered regions
• Maintained law and order

👥 District chiefs and junior chiefs administered lower areas.

title: 💰 Economy and Culture of Kafa
notes:
🌾 Economy:
• Agriculture
• Trade

🌱 Main crops:
• Coffee
• Enset

🛒 Major trade items:
• Ivory
• Musk
• Honey
• Coffee
• Enslaved people
• Gold

🛡️ Kafa used deep defensive trenches called Kuripo.

⛪ Christianity was introduced from Ennarya but remained mainly among the royal family, while most people continued indigenous religious practices.

title: 🌿 Yem State
notes:
The Yem had established a state before the late 16th century.

🏛️ Capital → Angari
👑 King → Tato or Amno

The Mowa dynasty ruled Yem until the late 19th century.

🏛️ Twelve councillors called Astessors assisted the king and were led by Waso.

Their responsibilities included:
• Selecting the successor
• Decisions concerning war
• Foreign relations
• Administration

Yem was influenced by Orthodox Christianity and had relations with the Christian Kingdom, but this relationship weakened after Oromo movement into the Gibe region.

title: 🏛️ Omotic States Under Kawo/Kati System
notes:
Major Omotic states included:
• Wolaita
• Gamo
• Gofa
• Dawuro
• Konta

👑 Wolaita, Gamo and Gofa → Kawo
👑 Dawuro and Konta → Kati

These states had broadly similar political structures but differed in administrative details.

title: 👑 Wolaita
notes:
📍 Located between the Bilate River and Omo River.

The ruling dynasty was called Wolaita Malla.

👑 Motalami was traditionally regarded as the first king of the Wolaita-Malla ruling family.

The dynasty was associated with Damot from the 13th century.

Later, the Tigre-Mala dynasty replaced Wolaita-Malla in the late 15th century and continued into the late 19th century.

Wolaita had tributary relations with the Christian Kingdom before these relations were disrupted by the Oromo movement.

title: 🏛️ Dawuro & Konta
notes:
🌿 Dawuro
Established in the 16th century according to tradition by the Kawuka clan.

By about 1700, the Kawuka dynasty had created a large state.

Famous rulers:
• Kati Erashu (1719–1775)
• Kati Halala (1775–1835)

🏛️ Dawuro administrative hierarchy:
Huduga → Abaliya → Danna → Guuda → Erasha → Woraba → Bushasha → Kate

🌿 Konta
The Khati supervised officials including:
• Gana
• Torancha
• Woraba
• Erasha
• Guda
• Dana

title: 🏔️ Gamo Political Organization
notes:
Gamo was organized into about 40–55 politically autonomous units called dere.

🏘️ Dere → autonomous political unit
👑 Kawo → hereditary ruler
🏛️ Duletha → assembly of the dere
👥 Halaka → elected officials and administrators

The king was the supreme head of the administrative system and could appoint or dismiss officials.

title: 🏛️ Other Omotic Political Systems
notes:
The highest authority among Basketo, Maleh, Kara, Zayise, Oyda and Kore was generally a hereditary king called Khati.

📌 Examples of administrative officials:
• Basketo → Dana, Guda, Bitena, Gudena, Chemach
• Maleh → Goda, Kagotoka, Katoydka
• Kara → Arti and Ghana
• Kore → Awajite, Daynena, Ushete, Tora Maga, Fizena and Mura

The exact duties and succession practices varied between societies.

title: 🌾 Omotic Economy, Land & Defense
notes:
🌱 Main economic activities:
• Agriculture
• Livestock raising
• Trade

🌾 Important crops:
• Enset
• Maize
• Taro
• Sorghum

🤝 Relations included both warfare and cooperation through trade and marriage.

🌳 Land ownership was organized around:
• Kinship
• Polity
• Social status

🛡️ Defensive fortifications were called Kella.

📍 Famous examples:
• Amado Kella in Wolaita
• Kati Halala Kella in Dawuro

title: ⚖️ Cushitic States & Peoples Under the Sera-Woma System
notes:
Several Highland East Cushitic peoples developed similar traditional political structures.

📌 Peoples included:
• Hadiya
• Kambata
• Sidama
• Tambaro
• Kabena
• Halaba
• Gedeo
• Konso
• Burji

⚖️ Sera → local cultural norms regulating communal social organization; it functioned as unwritten law.

👑 Woma → highest traditional authority in the system.

Decision-making was generally consultative and compromise-oriented.

title: 🏛️ Hadiya Traditional Administration
notes:
The Hadiya administrative system was called Sera.

👑 Adila/Garada → equivalent to king

The king led the council of elders.

📌 Clan organization:
• Each Giicho clan administered itself.
• Clan leaders used the title Garad.
• Garad was not an absolute ruler.
• Leadership could be based on personal qualities.

⚔️ Gatanna/Abegaz → elected war leader.

Hadiya's political and social structure was transformed by the wars of Imam Ahmed and Oromo population movement.

title: 🏔️ Kambata, Halaba, Tambaro & Sidama
notes:
🏔️ Kambata
Maintained a monarchical tradition from King Anno to King Dilbato. The rulers came from the Oyata clan.

⛰️ Mount Hambaricho was an important symbolic and ritual centre of Kambata.

🌿 Halaba
The Woma came from the Sidae clan.

🌿 Tambaro
Kings came from the Molla clans.

🌿 Sidama
Power transfer occurred through Luwa ceremonies every eight years. The Woma served as supreme judge and traditional authority.

title: 👥 Qabena, Gedeo & Konso Political Systems
notes:
👥 Qabena
• Ruled by elected Woma leaders
• Council of 12 judges
• Governed through traditional and Islamic law

🌿 Gedeo
• Traditional governance → Ballee
• Based on an age system
• Yaa → supreme council
• Abba Gadaa → political, social and ritual leadership
• Territorial units were administered by Roga

🏔️ Konso
• Decentralized political structure
• Poqalla → priest and peacemaker
• Council of elders participated in government
• Tella/Tselta → generation-set organization

title: 🌾 Enset Culture Complex
notes:
The southern Cushitic societies shared an important economic foundation known as the enset-culture complex.

🌱 Enset was a major staple crop for many groups.

📌 Benefits of enset cultivation:
• Provides carbohydrates
• Can be stored for months
• Supports dense population
• Complements cattle raising

Konso relied more heavily on cereals such as sorghum and millet because of its environment.

🏔️ Konso also developed sustainable terraced agriculture using stone terraces.

title: 🌿 Gurage Chiefdoms
notes:
The Gurage are not Cushitic-speaking, but their culture was strongly influenced by Cushitic-speaking peoples.

📍 Main areas:
• West of Lake Dambal
• Highlands of Dawaro

🌱 Main staple → Enset

👑 Local titles:
• Azmach
• Abegaz
• Nigus

🏛️ Basic political unit → Clan assembly

Political, social and legal authority was exercised by elected officials.

title: ⚖️ Gurage Sera Systems
notes:
The Gurage used traditional systems of law and governance.

📌 Sebat Bet → Yajoka Sera
📌 Kistane → Ye Gordana Sera

These systems involved:
• Justice
• Land administration
• Social organization
• Social events
• Political decision-making

Religious and ritual authorities helped legitimize the authority of political elders.

title: 🏛️ Siltie Sera
notes:
The Siltie developed a centralized traditional administrative system known as YeSiltie Sera.

👑 Supreme leader → Mule Gerad

📌 Important institutions:
• Abotgae → patrilineal descent
• Ummegae → mother lineage
• YeMule Siltie Melcho → general assembly
• Raga → judicial system

YeSiltie Sera also represented the norms and values regulating social, political and cultural life.

🌾 Economy:
• Mixed agriculture
• Enset in highlands
• Maize and wheat in lower areas
• Long-distance and caravan trade

title: 📌 8.1.2 WESTERN STATES
notes:
Western Ethiopia contained several Oromo monarchies, Leqa states, and peoples and sheikhdoms along the Ethio-Sudanese frontier.

📌 Major topics:
• Oromo Monarchies: Gibe States
• Oromo Monarchies: Leqa States
• Sheikhdoms and Peoples of Benishangul-Gumuz
• Local Chiefs of Gambella Peoples

title: 👑 Oromo Monarchies: Gibe States
notes:
The Oromo originally had an egalitarian and republican political organization based on the Gadaa system.

During expansion into Gibe and Wallaga, this system changed during the early 19th century.

📌 Causes of transformation:
• Shift from pastoralism to agriculture
• Class differentiation
• Continuous warfare
• Increased power of Abba Dula
• Control of land and markets
• Control of trade routes
• Private armies

War leaders gradually gained regional power and adopted the title Moti, meaning king.

title: 🗺️ Five Gibe States
notes:
Five major Oromo states emerged in the Gibe region:

1️⃣ Limmu-Ennarya
2️⃣ Jimma
3️⃣ Gumma
4️⃣ Gomma
5️⃣ Gera

📅 Emergence → mainly early 19th century

A similar development later occurred in Wallaga, where:
• Leqa Naqamte
• Leqa Qellem
emerged.

title: 🌿 Limmu-Ennarya
notes:
Limmu-Ennarya was the earliest Gibe state.

📍 Centre → Saqqa

It was established in the territory of the older Ennarya state.

🛤️ Strategic location allowed it to control long-distance trade routes linking the region with the north.

👑 Strongest ruler → Abba Bagibo/Ibsa
📅 Reign → 1825–1861

Under Abba Bagibo, Limmu-Ennarya reached the peak of its regional power.

title: 🕌 Jimma
notes:
Jimma became stronger than Limmu-Ennarya and other Gibe states during the middle of the 19th century.

👑 Famous ruler → Sanna/Abba Jifar I
📅 Reign → 1830–1855

Jimma's power was supported by:
• Islam
• Coffee trade
• Enslaved-person trade
• Commercial prosperity

Its success contributed to its supremacy in the second half of the 19th century.

title: 🏛️ Gumma, Gomma & Gera
notes:
🌿 Gumma
• Emerged during the first decade of the 19th century
• Became important around 1820
• Strong ruler → Oncho Jilcha
• Earliest Gibe state to accept Islam

🌿 Gomma
• One of the five Gibe states
• Participated in conflicts with neighboring states

🌿 Gera
• Became prominent around 1835
• Strong ruler → Tullu Gunji
• Known as a warrior king and administrator
• Had conflicts with Gumma

🕌 Gibe states generally converted from indigenous religions to Islam during the first half of the 19th century.

title: 🏛️ Oromo Monarchies: Leqa States
notes:
Two important monarchical centres emerged in Wallaga:

1️⃣ Leqa Naqamte
2️⃣ Leqa Qellem

🌿 Leqa Naqamte
Founder → Bakare Godana

Its power increased under:
• Moroda
• Kumsa Moroda

Kumsa later became Dejazmach Gabra-Egziabher after conversion to Christianity.

🌿 Leqa Qellem
Founder → Tullu
Successor → Jote

Jote consolidated the kingdom during the second half of the 19th century.

title: 💰 Economy of the Leqa States
notes:
The economy of the Leqa states was based on:

🌾 Agriculture
🛤️ Ethio-Sudanese frontier trade

Foreign merchants from the Funj Sultanate of Sudan visited the Leqa states.

Leqa Qellem under Jote Tullu maintained both hostile and peaceful relations with the Sheikhdoms of Asosa.

title: 🌿 Benishangul-Gumuz: Sheikhdoms & Peoples
notes:
📍 Located along the Ethio-Sudanese border.

The peoples mainly belonged to the Nilo-Saharan language family.

💰 The region was historically important for gold production.

🌾 Gumuz subsistence included shifting cultivation.

🔥 Slash-and-burn agriculture was used both for farming and natural-resource management.

🌳 Forests were highly valued and managed according to indigenous knowledge and beliefs.

title: 🌾 Gumuz Agriculture & Natural Resource Management
notes:
Gumuz farmers used knowledge of soil colour and drainage to identify fertile land.

🔥 Fire was used for:
• Hunting
• Encouraging new vegetation for livestock
• Reducing tsetse fly effects

🌱 Crop sequence:
1. Sorghum
2. Millet and sorghum
3. Cotton according to need

After three rounds, land was left fallow to allow forest regeneration.

title: 🌿 Shinasha
notes:
The Shinasha were one of the Gonga groups that established a powerful kingdom in southwestern Ethiopia before the 16th century.

📌 From the 16th century:
• Demographic and political pressure pushed them westward.
• Oromo expansion weakened and divided the Gonga kingdom.
• Southern group → Kafa
• Northern group → Shinasha

🌾 Subsistence:
• Shifting cultivation
• Cattle herding

👤 Cooperative shifting cultivation was coordinated by Dawa Nasho.

🌳 Shinasha culture strongly valued forest preservation.

title: 🏘️ Benishangul Political Organization
notes:
The Benishangul people practiced mixed farming.

🌾 Activities:
• Livestock raising
• Agriculture
• Trade
• Beekeeping
• Coffee cultivation

🍚 Staple food → Sorghum

🏛️ Administration was based on kinship lines and local leadership.

👥 Chiefs and councils of elders played important roles.

🕌 Islam spread through frontier trade and cultural relations with Sudanese communities.

🎵 Traditional musical instrument → Zumbara

title: 🛤️ Frontier Trade & Sheikhdoms
notes:
Benishangul-Gumuz peoples played an important role in frontier trade and cultural relations between Ethiopia and neighbouring regions.

🛒 Trade connected local peoples with Arabic-speaking merchants.

Muslim states formed in:
• Asosa
• Benishangul
• Khomosha

💰 Large gold deposits attracted outside interest.

The local Sheikhdoms defended their independence and territory.

title: 🌍 Gambella Peoples & Local Chiefs
notes:
Major peoples of Gambella included:
• Anywaa
• Nuer
• Majang
• Komo
• Opuo

The region did not have a strong centralized state structure.

👥 Anywaa:
• Political organization centered on villages
• Nyieye → noble
• Kuaari → headman
• Maintained peace and redistributed wealth

🌿 Majang:
• Traditionally egalitarian society
• Tapad → traditional leader
• Tapad mainly performed religious and ritual functions

title: 🌾 Gambella Economy & Trade
notes:
Gambella peoples lived mainly along rivers and cultivated floodplains.

🌾 Crops:
• Maize
• Tobacco
• Sorghum

🐟 Other activities:
• Fishing
• Hunting
• Gathering

🛤️ Trade connected Gambella with neighbouring regions.

Before the 1850s, manufactured goods from northern Sudan passed through Benishangul and Oromo territories and reached parts of South Sudan.

title: 📌 8.1.3 EASTERN STATES: HARAR, AFAR & SOMALI
notes:
The eastern region included important Islamic political centres and pastoral societies.

📌 Major topics:
• Harar
• Afar Sultanates
• Somali political organization

title: 🏙️ Harar & the Sultanate of Adal
notes:
After Ifat lost its independence, members of its ruling family moved toward Harar and established the Sultanate of Adal around 1380.

📍 Harar → political centre of Adal

Following Oromo expansion, Adal was reduced largely to the walled town of Harar.

After Imam Ahmed's death, Emir Nur Mujahid reorganized Muslim resistance.

📅 1559 → Nur Mujahid defeated and killed Gelawdewos.

However, Oromo forces had already reached Harar, forcing Nur to return and defend the city.

title: 🧱 Jegol Wall of Harar
notes:
As Oromo expansion occupied much of the surrounding area, Emir Nur Mujahid built a defensive wall around Harar.

🧱 Name → Jegol Wall

Harar was regarded as the “fourth holy city” of Islam.

The wall served as a protective barrier around the city.

Later, the Walasma rulers abandoned Harar and moved to Aussa.

title: 🕌 Harari Emirate
notes:
A local Harari dynasty established the Emirate of Harar in the middle of the 17th century.

👑 Founder → Emir Ali Ibn Dawd
📅 Reign → 1647–1662

Harar became:
• A centre of Islamic culture
• A political centre
• A major trade centre
• A centre of Islamic learning

It controlled trade routes linking the Gulf of Aden and Indian Ocean coast with the interior highlands.

📅 1875 → Egyptians occupied Harar for about a decade.
📅 1887 → Harar was incorporated into Menelik's Empire after the Battle of Chelanqo.

title: 🐪 Afar: Aussa, Bidu, Gobaad, Tajura & Rahaito
notes:
The Afar mainly inhabited the “Afar Triangle” covering:
• Ethiopia
• Eritrea
• Djibouti

The Afar are predominantly Muslim.

Their ancestors gradually shifted from farming and livestock raising in the highlands toward a more pastoral lifestyle.

🛤️ Important trading ports:
• Adulis
• Zula
• Obok
• Tajura

🧂 Afar land supplied Ethiopia with large quantities of rock salt called amole, which also served as currency for a long period.

title: 🏛️ Afar Sultanates
notes:
The Afar territory was historically organized into sultanates and semi-independent regions.

Major sultanates included:
• Aussa
• Bidu
• Tadjoura
• Rahaito
• Goobad

Each sultanate consisted of several villages and maintained its own political and cultural traditions.

title: 👑 Sultanate of Aussa
notes:
Aussa was initially ruled by local Afar chiefs who held the title Sultan.

📅 1577 → Imam Muhammed Ga'as moved the Adal capital from Harar to Aussa.

📅 1734 → Sultan Kadafo Hanfarie Aydahis established the Mudaito Sultanate.

The Mudaito clan subsequently ruled Aussa for a long period.

📌 Aussa was territorially larger than the other Afar sultanates.

title: ⚔️ Afar Political & Economic Power
notes:
Each Afar Sultan was both:
• Political leader
• Religious leader of his clan

Sultans:
• Controlled trade
• Taxed caravans
• Protected their territories

The Afar repeatedly resisted pressure from neighbouring highlanders and foreign powers.

🌍 Their coastal position exposed them to Ottoman, Egyptian and French intrusion.

title: 👥 The Somali
notes:
The Somali inhabited a large territory in the Horn of Africa.

🗣️ Language → Eastern Lowland Cushitic family

🌿 Livelihoods:
• Pastoralism
• Agriculture
• Trade

🏛️ Traditional political organization → Guurti

Guurti was a council of elders that handled:
• Criminal cases
• Civil cases
• Resource allocation
• Marriage
• Trade
• Conflict and crisis resolution

Adult males participated in decision-making, giving the system a highly democratic character.

title: 📌 8.2 GONDARINE PERIOD
notes:
🏙️ The Gondar Period refers to the period when the highland Christian Kingdom ruled from Gondar.

📅 Gondar founded as permanent capital → around 1636
👑 Founder → Fasiladas

The political centre had gradually shifted from the Shewan highlands toward Lake Tana because of:
• Adal's threat
• Oromo population movement

Gondar became the political centre for about two centuries.

title: 🏰 Foundation & Location of Gondar
notes:
Before Gondar became permanent capital, the rulers used mobile capitals.

📍 Temporary centres included:
• Denqez
• Gorgora
• Azezo
• Dembiya
• Qoga

Gondar was strategically located on trade routes linking:
• Southwestern Ethiopia
• Massawa on the Red Sea
• Mettema on the Ethio-Sudanese border

The permanent capital ended the tradition of ruling from temporary camps.

title: 🏛️ Gondarine Architecture & Achievements
notes:
Gondar became famous for architectural and technological achievements.

🏰 Major constructions:
• Castles
• Palaces
• Churches
• Bridges
• Swimming pools

The city experienced major prosperity under three successive rulers:

👑 Fasiladas (1632–1667)
👑 Yohannes I (1667–1682)
👑 Iyasu I (1682–1706)

Traditional schools of learning expanded around palaces and churches.

title: 🛒 Gondar as a Commercial & Urban Centre
notes:
Gondar developed important urban characteristics.

👥 Population → about 70,000

The population included different:
• Religious communities
• Cultural groups
• Indigenous communities
• Foreign communities

🛒 A daily market attracted merchants, craftsmen and rural people.

👤 Ethiopian Muslim merchants → Jeberti

🔨 Bete Israel were involved in crafts such as:
• Masonry
• Pottery
• Basketry
• Ironwork

title: 💰 Gondar Economy & Society
notes:
Gondar became a major commercial centre and encouraged strong urban-rural interaction.

📌 Developments included:
• Daily markets
• Craft production
• Long-distance trade
• Cash payment for labour services
• Urban growth

Separate living quarters existed for:
• Muslim communities
• Bete Israel
• Foreign communities from India, Greece, Armenia and Persia.

title: 📉 Decline of Gondar
notes:
After the first three strong Gondarine rulers, Gondar gradually declined.

📌 Causes included:
• Political disorder
• Social unrest
• Court intrigues
• Poisoning and assassinations
• Military weakness
• Growing regional warlords
• Weakening central authority
• Religious doctrinal conflicts within the Orthodox Tewahedo Church

After the assassination of Iyasu I in 1706, powerful regional warlords increasingly protected and influenced the imperial court.

title: 👑 Itege Mentewab
notes:
Itege Mentewab was an influential Quara-born woman during the later Gondarine period.

She was the wife of Emperor Bakafa and became regent for her young son Iyasu II after Bakafa's death.

👤 Supporter → Welde Leul
🏛️ Title given to Welde Leul → Ras Bitweded

Mentewab's political influence continued until she lost power to Ras Mikael Sehul in 1769.

title: 📌 8.3 ZEMENE-MESAFINT: THE ERA OF WARLORDS
notes:
📅 Zemene-Mesafint → 1769–1855

It refers to the period when actual political power was held by regional lords while the Gondarine monarchy became weak.

▶️ Beginning → Ras Mikael Sehul assassinated King Iyoas in 1769.
▶️ End → Kasa Hailu was crowned Tewodros II in 1855.

Major political regions included:
• Tigray
• Semen
• Debye
• Begemedir
• Lasta
• Yejju
• Wollo
• Gojjam
• Shewa

title: ⚔️ Beginning of Zemene-Mesafint
notes:
Between 1767 and 1769, political rivalry developed in Gondar between Wollo and Quara factions.

👩 Wubit → represented Wollo faction
👩 Itege Mentewab → represented Quara faction

After the death of Ras Bitweded Welde Leul in 1767, rivalry intensified.

Mentewab had strengthened relations with the Wollo Oromo through the marriage of her son Iyasu II to Wabi from a Wollo Oromo family.

In 1768, Mentewab invited Ras Mikael Sehul of Tigrai to restore order.

📅 1769 → Mikael Sehul assassinated King Iyoas, marking the beginning of the Zemene-Mesafint.

title: 👑 Ras Mikael Sehul
notes:
Ras Mikael Sehul was a powerful Tigrean regional lord.

💪 Sources of his power:
• Large army
• Modern firearms
• Access to Red Sea trade

He was given the title Ras Bitweded after restoring order in Gondar.

📅 1771 → Coalition of Gojjam, Amhara, Lasta and Wollo lords defeated him at Sarba-Kussa.

He returned to Tigrai and ruled there until his death in 1780.

title: ⚔️ Causes of Warlord Conflicts
notes:
Regional warlords fought each other mainly because they wanted to:

🏴 Expand their territories
💰 Control human and material resources
👑 Obtain the title of Ras Bitweded
🏛️ Become guardians of weak Gondarine kings
💰 Collect tribute in the name of the kings

Religious doctrinal conflicts within the Orthodox Tewahedo Church further intensified regional political struggles.

title: ⛪ Religious Conflict During Zemene-Mesafint
notes:
The Orthodox Tewahedo Church experienced intense doctrinal controversy.

📌 Effects:
• Divided the Church into factions
• Divisions acquired regional characteristics
• Weakened the Church
• Weakened the Ethiopian state
• Provided an ideological dimension to political conflicts
• Intensified the struggle among regional powers

title: 🌾 Social & Economic Effects of Zemene-Mesafint
notes:
The continuous wars severely affected peasants and the economy.

👨‍🌾 Peasants:
• Forced to feed armies
• Forced to supply bandits
• Farmlands became battlefields
• Villages were burned
• Agricultural production declined

🛒 Trade:
• Long-distance travel became dangerous
• Robbery increased
• Merchants paid heavy taxes at warlords' gates

Major trade items included:
• Ivory
• Gold
• Civet
• Enslaved people

title: 📉 Political Consequences of Zemene-Mesafint
notes:
The long period of regional warfare:

• Weakened the central monarchy
• Strengthened regional lords
• Reduced central political control
• Weakened agriculture
• Disrupted trade
• Caused human and material losses
• Weakened national power
• Undermined the sense of nationalism

📌 Zemene-Mesafint is therefore characterized by strong regionalism and weak central authority.

title: 📌 8.4 THE YEJJU DYNASTY
notes:
👑 Founder → Ali Gwangul (Ali I)
📅 Founded → 1786
🏛️ Also known as → Warra Sheh

The Yejju dynasty emerged after the defeat of Ras Mikael Sehul and dominated northern Ethiopian politics through puppet Gondarine kings.

📍 Major centres of political power:
• Gojjam
• Gondar
• Tigrai
• Wollo

🏛️ Main centre of Yejju power → Debre-Tabor

title: 👑 Ras Gugsa & Yejju Power
notes:
The Yejju dynasty reached its strongest position under Ras Gugsa.

📅 Reign → 1803–1825

Gugsa used:
• Military power
• Diplomacy
• Marriage relations

to exercise influence over:
• Gojjam
• Wollo
• Lasta
• Semen
• Wagara
• Dambya

He attempted to neutralize rival Tigrean rulers through diplomacy and marriage.

title: ⚔️ Yejju Challenges After Ras Gugsa
notes:
After Ras Gugsa died in 1825, the dynasty faced strong opposition from Semen and Tigrai.

👑 Ras Yemam → 1825–1828
• Defeated Semen's forces

👑 Ras Marye → succeeded Yemam in 1828

⚔️ 1831 → Battle of May-Aslamay near Debre Abay

Ras Marye and Dejazmach Sabagadis were killed.

🏆 The Yejju dynasty remained dominant.

title: 👑 Ras Ali II & End of Yejju Dominance
notes:
👑 Ras Ali Alula (Ali II)
📅 Reign → 1831–1853

Yejju political dominance over northern Ethiopia continued for about two more decades.

📌 Important events:
• 1826 → Yimam defeated Hayle-Mariam Gebre of Semen
• 1827 → Battle of Koso-Ber resulted in the death of Maru of Dambiya
• 1840s–1855 → Kasa Hailu fought to end the Zemene-Mesafint

📅 1855 → Kasa Hailu was crowned Tewodros II, ending the Zemene-Mesafint era.

title: 📌 8.5 THE KINGDOM OF SHEWA
notes:
The central highlands of Shewa had previously been a political centre of the Christian Kingdom.

The Christian state shifted its political centre toward Lake Tana because of:
• Adal pressure
• Oromo expansion

Strong Gondarine rulers, including Iyasu I, attempted to control Shewa through military expeditions.

Shewa gradually detached itself from the new Christian political centre.

title: 🏛️ Emergence of the Shewan Kingdom
notes:
During its period of isolation, Shewa became politically divided and several local chiefs emerged.

📅 Around the end of the 17th or beginning of the 18th century:
The Shewan kingdom emerged in Manz.

👑 Founder → local chief Negasi

During the Zemene-Mesafint, successive rulers consolidated the kingdom while remaining relatively isolated from the wars of northern Ethiopia.

🏛️ Centre → Ankober

title: 👑 Nigus Sahle Sellase
notes:
The Shewan Kingdom reached its height under Nigus Sahle Sellase.

📅 Reign → 1813–1847

Achievements:
• Expanded Shewan territory
• Brought several regions under Shewan control
• Maintained law and order
• Created political stability
• Encouraged foreign travellers to visit Shewa
• Established independent relations with Britain and France

title: 🌍 Shewa During Zemene-Mesafint
notes:
Shewa benefited from relative isolation from the wars of northern Ethiopia.

📌 Advantages:
• Greater political stability
• Consolidation of the kingdom
• Maintenance of law and order
• Territorial expansion
• Growth of foreign contacts
• Development of independent foreign relations

Shewa therefore became an important political centre during the later Zemene-Mesafint period.
